title: The EBA examines the use of stablecoins, including EMTs, in decentralised finance

sections.heading: The EBA examines the use of stablecoins, including EMTs, in decentralised finance

paras.loc: The EBA examines the use of stablecoins, including EMTs, in decentralised financ, para 1
The EBA examines the use of stablecoins, including EMTs, in decentralised financ, para 2

paras.text: Stablecoins, including e-money tokens (EMTs), play a central role in decentralised finance (DeFi) for borrowing, lending and trading and as a source of collateral.
paras.loc: The EBA examines the use of stablecoins, including EMTs, in decentralised financ, para 3

paras.text: Although DeFi adoption among EU consumers remains limited, access is becoming easier through crypto-asset service providers (CASPs) and AI-enabled applications.
paras.loc: The EBA examines the use of stablecoins, including EMTs, in decentralised financ, para 4

paras.text: The EBA identifies consumer protection and regulatory arbitrage risks and reiterates its recommendation that the European Commission assess whether additional requirements are needed for CASPs facilitating access to DeFi as part of the review of MiCA.
paras.loc: The EBA examines the use of stablecoins, including EMTs, in decentralised financ, para 5

paras.text: The European Banking Authority (EBA) today published a Report analysing the use of EMTs and other selected stablecoins in DeFi and the implications for consumers and supervisors. The EBA finds that stablecoins, including some EMTs issued under the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA), play a central role in the DeFi ecosystem by providing liquidity, collateral and settlement in DeFi trading and lending activities. The Report also highlights consumer protection, and regulatory arbitrage risks arising from the growing interaction between stablecoins and DeFi.
paras.loc: The EBA examines the use of stablecoins, including EMTs, in decentralised financ, para 6

paras.text: Although EU consumer participation in DeFi remains limited, access to these services is becoming increasingly straightforward. This is because of the growing role of CASPs in facilitating access to DeFi and offering products linked to DeFi activities, as well as increasing institutional interest in DeFi with 42% of European-based investors expecting to engage with DeFi by 2028. Developments in artificial intelligence, including AI agents, are also lowering barriers to entry for consumers.
paras.loc: The EBA examines the use of stablecoins, including EMTs, in decentralised financ, para 7

paras.text: The EBA highlights several risks arising from DeFi activities. Consumers may lose all their invested assets due to inadequate risk disclosures, highly leveraged positions, non-repayment of loaned stablecoins and operational vulnerabilities. The use of EMTs in DeFi may also create channels through which risks can be transmitted to issuers and to CASPs acting as gateways to DeFi ecosystems.
paras.loc: The EBA examines the use of stablecoins, including EMTs, in decentralised financ, para 8

paras.text: Additionally, the Report identifies potential risks of regulatory arbitrage. These include the use of DeFi structures to circumvent MiCA requirements relating to the offer to the public or admission to trading of EMTs in the European Union, as well as the prohibition on granting interest on EMTs.
paras.loc: The EBA examines the use of stablecoins, including EMTs, in decentralised financ, para 9

paras.text: Against this backdrop, the EBA reiterates the recommendation made in its response to the European Commission’s targeted consultation on the review of MiCA that the Commission assess whether additional regulatory requirements should apply to CASPs facilitating access to DeFi, in particular lending protocols.
paras.loc: The EBA examines the use of stablecoins, including EMTs, in decentralised financ, para 10

paras.text: The EBA will continue monitoring developments in the use of stablecoins in DeFi and will provide further evidence and technical input to the European Commission as appropriate.
paras.loc: The EBA examines the use of stablecoins, including EMTs, in decentralised financ, para 11

paras.text: The EBA contributes to the consistent application of Union law, promotes a common supervisory culture and helps prevent regulatory arbitrage under Article 8(1) of the EBA Founding Regulation. It also has a statutory duty to monitor and assess market developments, including technological innovation and innovative financial services, under Article 9(2).
paras.loc: Legal basis and background, para 1

paras.text: The 2026 EBA work programme on innovative applications included an analysis of how stablecoins are used on DeFi. The analysis aims to raise awareness of (i) trends in, and uses of, ARTs and EMTs in DeFi and (ii) the use of DeFi as a means to offer to the public in the EU non-MiCA tokens, potentially raising consumer protection and regulatory arbitrage concerns.
paras.loc: Legal basis and background, para 2

paras.text: MiCA regulates the activities of issuance, offer to the public and admission to trading of ARTs and EMTs, and the provision of crypto-asset services in the EU, but excludes from its scope services provided without an intermediary in a fully decentralised manner.
paras.loc: Legal basis and background, para 3

paras.text: DeFi is accessed typically via self-hosted wallets. Estimations show that usage of self-hosted wallets in EU Member States is marginal compared to other major financial centres. Furthermore, looking at locations with the highest interactions with DeFi, Germany, France and Spain rank first in the EU, but still respectively 18th, 19th and 26th on an international scale, behind countries such as India (1st), the US (2nd) and the UK (12th).
paras.loc: Legal basis and background, para 4
